prompt: I'm on the latest MapLibre GL JS. My style has a glyphs URL, and every label layer sets `text-font` to `["Roboto Regular"]`. Chinese place names render in the browser's default sans-serif. I want them drawn in Noto Sans SC, which I can host as a font file, without changing how the Latin labels look. How do I set that up?

Below is a **step-by-step recipe** that will let you keep the Latin labels in *Roboto* while drawing every Chinese label with *Noto Sans SC* – all without touching the rest of your style.

---

## 1.  Make the Noto Sans SC glyphs available to MapLibre

MapLibre (just like Mapbox GL JS) does **not** read a font file directly from the browser.  
It asks a *glyph-pbf* service for the glyphs it needs, using the URL you set in the top-level `glyphs` property of the style:

```json
{
  "glyphs": "https://my-fonts.example.com/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  …
}
```

So you have to:

1. **Download the TTF/OTF** for Noto Sans SC (Regular is enough for most maps).  
   ```bash
   curl -O https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-cjk/raw/main/Sans/OTF/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf
   ```

2. **Convert the TTF/OTF into the Mapbox glyph-pbf format**.  
   The easiest way is to use the `glyphs` CLI that ships with `@mapbox/fontnik` (or the newer `@mapbox/mbgl-glyphs`).

   ```bash
   # install the tool (once)
   npm i -g @mapbox/mbgl-glyphs

   # generate the whole Unicode range (0-65535) – you can limit it if you want
   mbgl-glyphs NotoSansSC-Regular.otf ./glyphs
   ```

   This creates a directory tree like:

   ```
   glyphs/
     Noto Sans SC Regular/
       0-255.pbf
       256-511.pbf
       …
   ```

3. **Serve the directory over HTTP** (any static file server will do).  
   Example with `python -m http.server`:

   ```bash
   cd glyphs
   python -m http.server 8080
   ```

   The glyphs are now reachable at  

   ```
   http://localhost:8080/Noto%20Sans%20SC%20Regular/0-255.pbf
   ```

4. **Add the new base URL to your style** (or replace the existing one if you host both Roboto and Noto there).

   ```json
   {
     "glyphs": "http://localhost:8080/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
     …
   }
   ```

   *Important*: The same base URL is used for **all** fonts, so you must also have the Roboto glyphs in the same directory structure (or point the URL to a place that already contains both). If you already have a glyph service that serves Roboto, just copy the `Noto Sans SC Regular` folder next to the existing `Roboto Regular` folder.

---

## 2.  Tell MapLibre *when* to use Noto Sans SC

MapLibre’s `text-font` property can be **data-driven**, i.e. an expression that decides which font stack to use for each feature.  
We’ll use the language tag that is already present in most vector-tile sources (`text_language` or the language-specific name fields). If your source does **not** contain a language tag, you can fall back to a simple regex that detects Chinese characters.

### 2.1  The simplest “fallback stack” (works if you don’t mind Noto providing Latin glyphs)

```json
"text-font": ["Noto Sans SC Regular", "Roboto Regular"]
```

MapLibre will try the first font; if a glyph is missing it falls back to the second.  
Because Noto Sans SC contains *all* Chinese glyphs **and** a full Latin set, this will make *all* labels use Noto, which is **not** what you asked for.

### 2.2  Language-aware expression (the recommended way)

Add an expression that picks the font **only when the feature’s language is Chinese**.

```json

  "case",
  // 1️⃣  Does the feature have a Chinese language tag?
  ["==", ["get", "text_language"], "zh"],          // Mapbox/MapLibre convention
  // → use Noto for Chinese
  ["Noto Sans SC Regular"],
  // 2️⃣  Otherwise keep the original Roboto
  ["Roboto Regular"]
]
```

If your tiles use the more explicit `name_zh`, `name_zh-Hans`, … fields instead of a `text_language` property, you can test for their existence:

```json
"text-font": [
  "case",
  ["any",
    ["has", "name_zh"],
    ["has", "name_zh-Hans"],
    ["has", "name_zh-CN"]
  ],
  ["Noto Sans SC Regular"],
  ["Roboto Regular"]
]
```

### 2.3  Pure-regex detection (when you have no language tag)

```json
"text-font": [
  "case",
  // Does the label contain at least one CJK Unified Ideograph?
  ["match",
    ["regexp_match", ["get", "name"], "[\\u4e00-\\u9fff]"],
    true,
    ["Noto Sans SC Regular"],
    ["Roboto Regular"]
  ]
]
```

> **Tip** – `regexp_match` is a MapLibre expression that returns a boolean.  
> The Unicode range `\u4e00-\u9fff` covers the “common” Chinese characters.

---

## 3.  Apply the expression to every label layer

You can edit each label layer manually, but it’s easier to let a script do it (or use the style editor in MapLibre Studio / Mapbox Studio).  
Below is a **minimal example** of a typical `place-label` layer that you would find in an OpenMapTiles-based style.

  "type": "symbol",

    "text-size": 12,
    "text-anchor": "center",
    "text-allow-overlap": false
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#222"
  }
}
```

Do the same for any other symbol layer that shows place names, road names, POI labels, etc.

They request *glyph-pbf* files from a URL that looks like  

```
https://my-fonts.com/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf

* **{range}** is a Unicode range block (`0-255`, `256-511`, … up to `65536-65535`).

```bash

npm i -g @mapbox/ttf2pbf   # or use the mapbox/fontnik binary if you prefer
```

```bash

# … continue until you have covered the whole CJK range (0-65535 is safe)
```

```

       0-255.pbf
       256-511.pbf
       512-767.pbf
       …

MapLibre will try the fonts **in order** and will fall back to the next one **only for the glyphs that are missing** in the previous font.

Then you can write: ```json "text-font": [ "case", ["==", ["get", "text_language"], "zh"], // Chinese (both zh-CN and zh-TW are “zh”) ["Noto Sans SC Regular"], // → use Noto for Chinese ["Roboto Regular"] // → otherwise use Roboto ] ``` #### b) When you only have the name field If your tiles only have a `name` (or `name_zh`) field, you can detect Chinese characters with a regular-expression match: ```json "text-font": [ "case", [ "any", ["match", ["get", "name"], ["zh"], true, false], // explicit zh name field ["regexp_match", ["get", "name"], "[\\u4e00-\\u9fff]"] // any CJK ideograph ], ["Noto Sans SC Regular"], ["Roboto Regular"] ] ``` > `\\u4e00-\\u9fff` covers the “CJK Unified Ideographs” block, which contains virtually all common Chinese characters. #### c) Put the expression into every label layer You only need to edit the **layout** of the layers that draw place/road/poi labels (usually `symbol` layers).
